52.text:
Opinions are divided as to whether individuals should be responsible for healthy eating or whether society and governments should take action. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of personal responsibility argue that people make the daily choices that shape their own health. Nobody can eat on someone else's behalf, and many illnesses linked to diet, such as type 2 diabetes and heart disease, are largely preventable through sensible habits. Adults can read labels, cook simple meals and limit sweets and fried food, and parents set the example for their children at home. A person who chooses fruit and water instead of biscuits and fizzy drinks, for example, lowers their own risk of illness without needing any law. Taking responsibility also respects personal freedom and encourages independence.

On the other hand, advocates of government action point out that individual choices are shaped by the environment in which people live. Cheap, heavily advertised, high-calorie food is available on every street, while fresh produce can be expensive or hard to find in poorer areas. People who work long hours or live on low incomes may have little time or money to cook healthy meals. Governments can use education, clear labelling, advertising rules, school meal standards and taxes to make the healthy option the easy and affordable one. A child who is offered a nutritious school lunch every day, for instance, develops better habits without depending on family income.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that the most effective approach combines official leadership with personal action, since governments should shape the food environment while individuals make the daily choices that determine their health.

132.text:
Heart disease, diabetes and many other illnesses have been linked to the way people live, and opinions differ on who should be responsible for health: individuals themselves, or society and the government. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of personal responsibility argue that people make the daily choices that shape their own health. Smoking, drinking too much alcohol, eating badly, sleeping too little and avoiding exercise account for a large share of preventable illness, and no doctor can undo years of unhealthy habits. Motivation also has to come from within: a person who is determined to stop smoking and walks every day is far more likely to stay well than one who waits to be told what to do. Individuals who look after themselves also reduce the burden on the health service and save money. A man who quits cigarettes at forty, for example, may add years to his life and avoid costly treatment later.

On the other hand, advocates of government action point out that individuals cannot control many of the things that affect their health. Clean water, vaccination, safe workplaces and cleaner air depend on public policy, and screening programmes and hospitals require national planning and funding. Poorer people often face higher risks, since they may live in damp housing or have less access to doctors. A vaccination programme, for example, protects a whole community in a way that no individual could arrange alone. Governments can also restrict tobacco sales and give reliable health information.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Personally, I believe that governments should provide the system and the safeguards, while individuals use them wisely and take care of themselves.

394.text:
The cost of modern medicine is rising, and people disagree about who should pay for it: individuals themselves, or society through the government. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of individual payment argue that people should take responsibility for the cost of their own care. When patients pay something, even a small fee, they tend to use services more carefully, which reduces waste and unnecessary visits. Individual payment can also keep taxes lower and allows people to choose the level of cover that suits them. Competition between private providers may improve quality and shorten waiting times, since clinics must attract patients. A small charge for a routine consultation, for example, may discourage people from seeing a doctor for minor complaints that could be treated at home, leaving more time for those who are seriously ill.

On the other hand, advocates of public funding point out that illness is unpredictable and expensive, so the cost of care should be shared. A serious illness can ruin a family's finances through no fault of its own, and people who delay treatment because they cannot pay often need costlier emergency care later. Public funding protects the poor, keeps the workforce healthy and treats health as a basic right rather than a luxury. A patient who cannot afford cancer treatment, for instance, may lose both health and savings. Shared funding spreads the risk across the whole population, so that no one is left without help.

In conclusion, both views have merit. Overall, I believe that society should fund essential care, with modest personal contributions for non-urgent services, because this protects the vulnerable while limiting waste.

367.text:
Obesity and diet-related disease are rising in many countries, and some people believe that healthy eating should be promoted through taxation on unhealthy foods. Others disagree. This essay will consider both perspectives before explaining my own opinion.

On the one hand, supporters of such a tax argue that it sends a clear price signal. Higher prices reduce consumption of sugary drinks and snacks, encourage manufacturers to reduce sugar and fat in their recipes, and raise revenue that can be spent on health services. Some countries that taxed sugary drinks saw sales fall and recipes change, which suggests that the policy can work. Taxes are also cheaper to run than many other measures, since they use the existing tax system. A tax on soft drinks, for example, can persuade a company to cut the sugar in its best-selling product rather than pay more. If the money is used to subsidise fruit and vegetables or to fund school meals, the benefit is greater still.

On the other hand, critics point out that taxes on food hit poorer households hardest. People on low incomes spend a larger share of their money on food, and they may simply switch to another cheap unhealthy product, so the higher price alone does not improve their diet. Taxes may also seem unfair, as they punish people instead of helping them. Education, better access to fresh food and clear labels may achieve more in the long run. A family that lives far from a market selling fresh vegetables, for instance, will not eat better just because chips cost more.

To sum up, both positions have their merits; nevertheless, I believe that a tax can be useful if its revenue is used to make healthy food cheaper and more accessible, rather than as a punishment alone.

260.text:
Many children pass fast-food outlets on their way to and from school, and some people argue that governments should regulate them. I largely agree, since children are especially vulnerable to cheap, convenient fast food near their school, although rules should be fair to small businesses.

To begin with, children are especially vulnerable to cheap, convenient fast food near their school. Young people have little money, little self-control and habits that are still forming, so an outlet at the school gate makes unhealthy eating the default. Pupils who buy chips and fizzy drinks from a shop next to the school every lunchtime, for example, take in far more sugar and fat than they realise. Childhood obesity is rising in many countries, and it can lead to diabetes and heart problems later in life. Restricting nearby outlets reduces temptation and supports the healthy meals that schools provide.

Furthermore, only governments can set rules that apply to everyone. Parents and teachers can advise children, but they cannot control what is sold outside the gate, and a single outlet that changes its menu may lose customers to a rival. Planning rules, such as limiting new outlets within a certain distance of schools, create a level playing field and send a clear message about public health. However, regulation is not enough on its own. Pupils can still buy food elsewhere, and small businesses depend on their income, so existing outlets should be given time and support to offer healthier options. Education about nutrition and good school meals are also needed so that children make better choices even when temptation exists.

In conclusion, governments should regulate fast-food outlets near schools to a large extent, because children are vulnerable and habits form early, provided that the rules are fair and combined with education.
